[[EADS/Northrop Grumman KC-45]] }} The '''Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport''' ('''MRTT''') is a [[Europe]]an [[aerial refueling]] and [[military transport aircraft]] based on the civilian [[Airbus A330]]. A total of 17 countries have placed firm orders for approximately 85 aircraft, of which 66 have been delivered. A version of the A330 MRTT, the [[EADS/Northrop Grumman KC-45]], was selected by the [[United States Air Force]] for its [[KC-X|aerial tanker replacement program]], but lost when the program was rebid. According to Airbus, the A330 MRTT has more than 90% of the air-to-air refueling aircraft market share outside the United States. ==Design and development== [[File:Yoyager-underwing-cobham-pod.jpg|thumb|right|Starboard refuelling pod on a [[Royal Air Force]] (RAF) Voyager]] [[File:Refuelling boom on RAAF A330 MRTT.JPG|thumb|Centre refuelling boom under the tail of a RAAF KC-30A]] [[File:Refueling terminal in a RAAF KC-30.jpg|thumb|right|RAAF KC-30A refuelling control station. Refuelling systems are controlled by an operator in the cockpit, who can view the refuelling on 2D and 3D screens.]] [[File:Airbus A330-MRTT construction-4.jpg|thumb|The A330 MRTT cabin can be reconfigured to carry passengers.]] [[File:VIP interior of RAF Voyager (2).jpg |thumb|VIP interior]] The Airbus A330 MRTT is a military derivative of the [[Airbus A330|A330-200]] airliner. It is designed as a dual-role air-to-air refuelling and transport aircraft. For air-to-air refuelling missions, the A330 MRTT can be equipped with a combination of any of the following systems:{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}} * Refuelling other aircraft ** Airbus Military Aerial Refuelling Boom System (ARBS) for [[Aerial refueling#Flying boom|receptacle-equipped]] receiver aircraft. ** [[Cobham plc|Cobham]] 905E under-wing refuelling pods for [[Aerial refueling#Probe-and-drogue|probe-equipped]] receiver aircraft. ** Cobham 805E Fuselage Refuelling Unit (FRU) for probe-equipped receiver aircraft * Being refuelled ** Universal Aerial Refuelling Receptacle Slipway Installation (UARRSI) for self in-flight refuelling. The A330 MRTT has a maximum fuel capacity of {{Convert|111000|kg|lb|abbr=on}} without the use of additional fuel tanks, leaving space for {{Convert|45000|kg|lb|abbr=on}} of additional cargo. The A330 MRTT's wing has common structure with the four-engine [[Airbus A340|A340-200/-300]] with reinforced mounting locations and provision for fuel piping for the A340's outboard engines. The A330 MRTT's wing therefore requires little modification to use these [[hardpoint]]s for the [[Aerial refueling#Probe and Drogue Operation|wing refuelling pods]].[http://www.airforce-technology.com/projects/a330_200/ A330-200 Future Strategic Tanker Aircraft (FSTA)—Multi-Role Tanker Transporter (MRTT), Europe] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080523162446/http://www.airforce-technology.com/projects/a330_200/ |date=23 May 2008}}. Airforce-technology.com.{{Unreliable source?|reason=domain on WP:BLACKLIST|date=June 2016}} The A330 MRTT cabin can be modified to carry up to 380 passengers in a single-class configuration, allowing a complete range of configurations from maximised troop transport to complex customisation suitable for VIP and guest missions. Available configurations include 300 passengers in a single class and 266 passengers in two classes.{{cite web|url=http://militaryaircraft-airbusds.com/Portals/0/Images/Aircraft/a330/about/A330MRTTBrochure2014.pdf|title=A330 MRTT: The Benchmark|access-date=17 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160207150805/http://militaryaircraft-airbusds.com/Portals/0/Images/Aircraft/a330/about/A330MRTTBrochure2014.pdf|archive-date=7 February 2016|url-status=live}} The A330 MRTT can also be configured to perform Medical Evacuation (Medevac) missions; up to 130 standard stretchers can be carried. The main deck cargo configuration allows carriage of standard commercial containers and pallets, military, ISO and NATO pallets (including seats) and containers, and military equipment and other large items which are loaded through a cargo door. Like the A330-200, the A330 MRTT includes two lower deck cargo compartments (forward and aft) and a bulk area capability. The cargo hold has been modified to be able to transport up to eight military pallets in addition to civilian [[unit load device]]s (ULDs).{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}} An optional [[crew rest compartment]] (CRC) can be installed in the forward cabin, accommodating a spare crew to increase time available for a mission. The passenger cabin of the A330 MRTT can be provided with a set of removable [[airstair]]s to enable embarkation and disembarkation when [[jet bridge]]s or ground support equipment are not available.{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}} Standard commercial A330-200s are delivered from Airbus's Final Assembly Line in [[Toulouse]], [[France]] to the [[Airbus Military]] Conversion Centre in [[Getafe]], [[Spain]] for fitting of refuelling systems and military avionics. The tanker was certified by Spanish authorities in October 2010.{{cite web|url=http://www.flightglobal.com/articles/2010/10/06/348171/a330-tanker-gains-military-certification.html|title=A330 tanker gains military certification|date=6 October 2010|access-date=7 October 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101007211622/http://www.flightglobal.com/articles/2010/10/06/348171/a330-tanker-gains-military-certification.html|archive-date=7 October 2010|url-status=live}} The first delivered aircraft (the third to be converted) arrived in Australia on 30 May 2011 and was formally handed over to the [[Royal Australian Air Force]] (RAAF) two days later on 1 June.{{cite web|url=http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/06/first-raaf-kc-30-arrives/|publisher=Australian Aviation|date=1 June 2011|access-date=27 June 2011|title=First RAAF KC-30 arrives|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605055911/http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/06/first-raaf-kc-30-arrives/|archive-date=5 June 2011|url-status=live}} On 30 September 2016, [[Airbus Defence and Space]] completed the first flight of the ''new standard'' A330 MRTT. The new standard features structural modifications, aerodynamic improvements for a 1% fuel-burn reduction, upgraded avionics computers, and enhanced military systems. The first delivery was planned for 2018.{{cite web|url=https://airbusdefenceandspace.com/newsroom/news-and-features/first-new-standard-a330-mrtt-makes-maiden-flight/|title=First new standard A330 MRTT makes maiden flight|website=airbusdefenceandspace.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161013083234/https://airbusdefenceandspace.com/newsroom/news-and-features/first-new-standard-a330-mrtt-makes-maiden-flight/|archive-date=13 October 2016}} An Airbus/[[Saab AB|Saab]] team proposed an A330-based [[Airborne early warning and control]] (AEW&C) ("AWACS") variant with Saab's [[Erieye]] radar to the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|UK's Ministry of Defence]] in 2018 for the replacement of its [[Boeing E-3 Sentry]] fleet.{{cite web|date=15 November 2018|title=UK MoD: Other bidders didn't have a chance against Boeing Wedgetail|url=https://www.defensenews.com/air/2018/11/15/uk-mod-other-bidders-didnt-have-a-chance-against-boeing-wedgetail/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240322024317/https://www.defensenews.com/air/2018/11/15/uk-mod-other-bidders-didnt-have-a-chance-against-boeing-wedgetail/|archive-date=22 March 2024|access-date=22 March 2024|work=Defense News|publisher=Sightline Media Group}} The boom operators sit at a video console using the Boom Enhanced Vision System. It uses a 3D camera vision system for day and night vision and ergonomics are significantly improved compared to operating in a prone position.{{cite web|title=Kappa Vision System for A330 MRTT|url=https://www.kappa-optronics.com/en/aviation/in-flight-refueling-vision-systems/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240322024558/https://www.kappa-optronics.com/en/aviation/in-flight-refueling-vision-systems/|archive-date=22 March 2024|access-date=28 September 2022}} ===A330 MRTT+=== In November 2023, Airbus began derisking studies for an updated MRTT based on the [[A330neo]], noting that A330-200 production ended in 2018 and very few airframes remain available for MRTT use. In particular, the company studied the feasibility of fitting the pods for the probe-and-drogue refuelling system onto the A330neo's new wing.{{cite news|last1=Perry|first1=Dominic|date=21 November 2023|title=Airbus begins derisking studies for A330neo-based tanker|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/defence/airbus-begins-derisking-studies-for-a330neo-based-tanker/155932.article|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20231121182154/https://www.flightglobal.com/defence/airbus-begins-derisking-studies-for-a330neo-based-tanker/155932.article|archive-date=21 November 2023|access-date=22 March 2024|work=Flight Global}} The new variant, dubbed MRTT+, was announced at the 2024 [[Farnborough Air Show]]. Based on the A330-800, and powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines, the MRTT+ achieves 8% better fuel efficiency than the original MRTT.{{cite news|last1=Donale|first1=David|title=Airbus A330 Multi-Role Tanker Transport Goes Neo {{!}} AIN|url=https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/defense/2024-07-24/airbus-a330-multi-role-tanker-transport-goes-neo|work=Aviation International News|date=24 July 2024}}{{cite news|title=A330 MRTT: the evolution of the world's leading air-to-air refuelling tanker|url=https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/stories/2024-09-a330-mrtt-the-evolution-of-the-worlds-leading-air-to-air-refuelling-tanker|work=www.airbus.com|date=13 September 2024|access-date=16 September 2024}} The first MRTT+ rolled out of the assembly line in September 2026.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-09-12 |title=Toulouse, le premier Airbus A330 MRTT+ est sorti ! |url=https://www.avianews.ch/post/toulouse-le-premier-airbus-a330-mrtt-est-sorti |access-date=2026-09-12 |website=Avia news |language=fr}} ==Operational history== The A330 MRTT has been ordered by Australia, France, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, Canada, and by [[NATO]] in a multi-nation deal. Australia was the launch customer for the A330 MRTT. According to Airbus, the A330 MRTT has more than 90% in air-to-air refueling aircraft market outside the United States.{{cite news |last1=Ruitenberg |first1=Rudy |title=Airbus mulls boosting tanker production on 'very high' demand |url=https://www.defensenews.com/global/europe/2025/06/18/airbus-mulls-boosting-tanker-production-on-very-high-demand/ |access-date=30 June 2025 |work=Defense News Australia initially arranged to procure four MRTTs with an option to obtain a fifth; this option for a fifth was exercised to allow for two simultaneous deployments of two aircraft, the fifth being for contingency coverage. Australian KC-30As are operated by [[No. 33 Squadron RAAF]], based at [[RAAF Base Amberley]] near Brisbane in Queensland. In 2005, the RAAF expected deliveries to begin in 2008 and end in 2010.{{cite news|title=New tankers to take on many roles|url=http://www.defence.gov.au/news/raafnews/editions/4702/topstories/story12.htm|work=Air Force News (Australia)|date=24 February 2005|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514101526/http://www.defence.gov.au/news/raafnews/EDITIONS/4702/topstories/story12.htm|archive-date=14 May 2011}} Deliveries fell two years behind schedule, partly due to boom development issues.[http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/01/boom-or-bust-raaf-kc-30-loses-boom/ Boom or bust! – RAAF KC-30 loses boom] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110815124800/http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/01/boom-or-bust-raaf-kc-30-loses-boom/ |date=15 August 2011}}. Australian Defence Magazine|url=https://www.australiandefence.com.au/news/multi-billion-dollar-investment-in-new-c-130j-hercules-aircraft|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240322025716/https://www.australiandefence.com.au/defence/air/multi-billion-dollar-investment-in-new-c-130j-hercules-aircraft|archive-date=22 March 2024|access-date=24 July 2023|work=Australian Defence Magazine|language=en}} ===United Kingdom=== {{main|Future Strategic Tanker Aircraft}} In January 2004, the UK [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]] announced the selection of an A330 MRTT variant to provide tanking for the RAF for the next 30 years under the [[Future Strategic Tanker Aircraft]] (FSTA) programme, replacing the RAF's [[Lockheed TriStar (RAF)|TriStar]] and [[Vickers VC10|VC10]] tankers. The Ministry of Defence entered negotiations with the EADS-led AirTanker consortium. On 27 March 2008, a deal was signed to lease 14 MRTTs under a [[private finance initiative]] arrangement with AirTanker, with the first to enter service in 2011.{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/7316835.stm|title=EADS wins £13bn RAF tanker deal|work=BBC News|date=27 March 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080402231104/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/7316835.stm|archive-date=2 April 2008|url-status=live}} The service's annual cost, including military personnel costs is around £450 million for a delivery of 18,000 flying hours{{Cite web|last=Committee of Public Accounts|date=8 September 2010|title=Delivering Multi-Role Tanker Aircraft Capability|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm201011/cmselect/cmpubacc/425/425.pdf|website=Parliament.UK}} a rate of approximately £25,000 per hour. {{flag|Spain}} : [[Spanish Air and Space Force]] – 3 ordered (order not listed in Airbus O&D report as of 31 August 2026). ; {{flag|Thailand}} : [[Royal Thai Air Force]] – RTAF has ordered an Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport Plus (MRTT+), the final delivery to customer in 2029.{{cite web |date=25 September 2025 |title=Royal Thai Air Force orders next generation Airbus A330 MRTT+ |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-09-royal-thai-air-force-orders-next-generation-airbus-a330-mrtt |access-date=25 September 2025 |website=Airbus}} ==Accidents and incidents== On 19 January 2011, an air refuelling accident occurred between a boom-equipped A330 MRTT and a Portuguese Air Force [[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon]] over the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Portugal. Early reports indicated that the boom broke off at the aft end of the boom near the F-16's receptacle, causing the boom to recoil into the MRTT's underside. The boom then became uncontrollable and oscillated until it broke off the boom assembly at the pivot point. Both aircraft were damaged but landed safely.{{Cite news|url=http://www.flightglobal.com/articles/2011/01/20/352119/airbus-a330-tanker-damaged-in-refuelling-mishap.html|title=Airbus A330 tanker damaged in refuelling mishap|work=[[Flight International]]|date=20 January 2011|first=Craig|last=Hoyle|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110123013954/http://www.flightglobal.com/articles/2011/01/20/352119/airbus-a330-tanker-damaged-in-refuelling-mishap.html|archive-date=23 January 2011|url-status=live}} The A330 MRTT involved was an Airbus test aircraft destined for the RAAF, operated by an Airbus crew. At the time of the incident, Airbus had not yet begun deliveries.{{Cite news|url=http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/01/boom-or-bust-raaf-kc-30-loses-boom/|work=Australianaviation.com.au|title=Boom or bust! – RAAF KC-30 loses boom|date=20 January 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110815124800/http://australianaviation.com.au/2011/01/boom-or-bust-raaf-kc-30-loses-boom/|archive-date=15 August 2011|url-status=live}} On 10 September 2012, an A330 MRTT's refuelling boom detached in flight at an altitude of {{convert|27,000|ft|abbr=on}} in Spanish airspace.{{R|"Flightglobal1"|"AviationWeek1"}} The boom separated cleanly at a mechanical joint and fell to the ground, while the tanker landed safely in [[Getafe]] without any injuries.{{R|"Flightglobal1"|"AviationWeek1"}} The fault was attributed to a conflict between the backup boom hoist (fitted to the UAE-destined MRTTs) and the primary boom retraction mechanism, as well as to the test conducted.{{R|"Flightglobal1"}} Airbus later explained that the malfunction was not possible under ordinary operating conditions, and that procedures had been implemented to avoid similar incidents in the future.{{R|"Flightglobal1"}} Following the incident, the ''[[Instituto Nacional de Técnica Aeroespacial]]'', Spain's airworthiness authority, issued precautionary restrictions to other users of boom-equipped A330s. On 9 February 2014, a [[Royal Air Force]] A330 MRTT Voyager carrying 189 passengers and 9 crew from [[RAF Brize Norton]] to [[Camp Bastion]] suddenly lost {{convert|4,440|ft|abbr=on}} of altitude in 27 seconds and reaching a maximum descent rate of {{convert|15000|ft/min|abbr=on}} while the co-pilot was out of the cockpit.{{Cite news|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/camera-trouble-led-to-raf-voyager-grounding-investigation-finds/112702.article|work=flightglobal.com|title=Camera trouble led to RAF Voyager grounding, investigation finds|date=19 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202055343/https://www.flightglobal.com/camera-trouble-led-to-raf-voyager-grounding-investigation-finds/112702.article|archive-date=2 February 2023|url-status=live}} The sudden descent caused several injuries to passengers and crew, some of whom struck the ceiling of the aircraft. The co-pilot returned to the cockpit, regained control, and the aircraft diverted to [[Incirlik Air Base]] and landed without further incident. The incident resulted in the grounding of the entire RAF Voyager fleet for 12 days until it was determined that the event was caused by the captain's improperly stowed [[DSLR]] camera being jammed between the captain's armrest and the side-stick, forcing the stick forward when the captain adjusted his seat forward.{{Cite web|title=Service Inquiry: incident involving Voyager ZZ333 on 9 February 2014|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/service-inquiry-incident-involving-voyager-zz333-on-9-february-2014|access-date=8 May 2023|website=GOV.UK|date=23 March 2015|language=en}} On 20 June 2025, members of the [[Palestine Action]] activist group infiltrated RAF Brize Norton in an act of protest towards the [[United Kingdom and the Gaza war|United Kingdom's support]] of Israeli [[Gaza war]] actions. The group sprayed red paint on the airframes and engines of two MRTTs using tools such as a modified [[fire extinguisher]].{{Cite web |title=Pro-Palestinian activists say they damaged planes at UK military base |url=https://www.lbcgroup.tv/news/world-news/862306/lbci-lebanon-articles/en |access-date=2025-06-20 |website=LBCIV7 |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Pro-Palestinian activists break into RAF base and 'vandalise' aircraft |url=https://news.sky.com/story/pro-palestinian-activists-break-into-raf-base-and-vandalise-aircraft-13386065 |access-date=2025-06-20 |website=Sky News |language=en}} The grounding of the aircraft,{{Citation needed|date=July 2025|reason=News source stating that the aircraft were grounded, or contradictory statement (in which case change the prose)}}{{Clarify|reason=Airframe number if available|date=July 2025}} which were stated to be damaged, would not impact the RAF's mission; with Armed Forces Minister [[Luke Pollard]] stating that "the activities of the RAF were unaffected".{{cite web |last1=West |first1=Lisa |title=Government say RAF 'unaffacted' by damage to tankers |url=https://ukdefencejournal.org.uk/government-say-raf-unaffacted-by-damage-to-tankers/ |website=ukdefencejournal.org.uk |date=25 June 2025 |publisher=UK Defence Journal |access-date=19 July 2025}} ==Specifications== {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; font-size:92%" |- style="vertical-align:top" | style="background:#EAECF0; border-top:solid 2px black; border-left:solid 2px black; border-bottom:solid 2px grey; width:20%" | '''Parameters''' | style="text-align:center; border-top:solid 2px black; border-left:solid 2px grey; border-bottom:solid 2px grey; width:40%; background:#EAECF0" | '''A330 MRTT'''
